Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder at kodely.me).

TASK: a second batch of SEO articles, plus corrections to live content that is currently wrong.

## Read the existing pipeline first — it is built and working, do not rebuild it
`scripts/seo/lib.mjs`, `scripts/seo/validate.mjs`, `scripts/seo/seed.mjs`, and the 17 existing articles in `content/seo/`. The validator runs 20+ checks and the seeder is idempotent with a `--dry-run` diff. Match the existing article format exactly.

## PART 1 — corrections to LIVE content (do this first, it matters more than new articles)
56 posts are live on kodely.me. Two known problems:

1. **A wrong credit figure.** Batch-1 posts state *"A typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits."* Measurements are 144 and 472 credits — the second is over 3x the top of that range. **Remove the number entirely; do not replace it with another number.** `estimateCredits`'s own comment says two samples is not a distribution. On a product whose headline promise is no bill shock, an understated public cost figure is the worst thing to be wrong about.
2. **An export claim that inverts on deploy.** Several posts say *"there's no zip or full-project download."* That is TRUE in production today — `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts` is built but NOT deployed. It becomes false the moment it ships, and `kodely-vs-rocket-new` and `kodely-vs-lovable` both list "Export / download code — Not yet" in their comparison tables.

For each: the source of live content is the `BlogPost` table on the production box, not this repo. `seo-batch1.json` is the local source for batch 1. Produce corrected article data plus a clear written procedure for applying it to prod, and flag prominently that the export corrections must ship **in the same window as the deploy**, not after.

Also re-read with fresh eyes and report on: `website-builder-for-dentists`, `website-builder-for-chiropractors`, `website-builder-for-photographers`, `build-a-booking-appointment-website-with-ai`. Their keyword intent is appointment booking, patient forms and photo galleries — none of which the builder can produce. (`build-a-online-store-with-ai` was already checked and IS honest about having no cart; do not assume the others are.)

## PART 2 — 12-18 new articles
**Ground every capability claim in code before writing it.** `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM (read in full — it now forbids inventing business facts and forbids controls that only pretend to work), `lib/foundation.ts`, `app/api/site/[slug]/**` (the CSP), `lib/credits.ts`, `lib/assets/` (461 inlinable assets now exist — that is a genuine, newly-true angle), `lib/site-seo.ts`.

The previous agent produced a list of topics that CANNOT be written truthfully — needing backend, form delivery, e-commerce, image upload, multi-page routing, custom domains, relaxed CSP, or `font-src`. Do not write those. Prefer honest, high-intent topics: buildable verticals scoped to one-page credibility sites with link-out CTAs, how-it-works explainers, and comparisons where you speak only factually about Kodely's own side.

Do not invent statistics, testimonials, customer counts or awards. **Publish no per-build credit figure anywhere.**

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `content/seo/` AND `scripts/seo/`
Do NOT edit `app/blog/**` (read it to learn the render contract), `seo-batch1.json` may be read but produce corrections as new data files rather than editing it in place if that is cleaner — your call, state it.

## Constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- Run the validator on everything. `--dry-run` the seeder freely; a real local write is fine only if idempotent and you do not delete rows you did not create.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean.** Parallel agents are running — errors in files you did not touch are not yours.

## Report back
The corrections with exact before/after text and the procedure to apply them to prod, your verdict on the four suspect live posts, the new articles with the code file grounding each claim, and anything you could not write truthfully.

- hyperframes: Mandatory entry point: read this first for any request to make, create, edit, animate, or render a video, animation, or motion graphic, including a promo, explainer, captioned clip, title card, overlay, slideshow or interactive deck, Remotion port, or any HyperFrames HTML composition. Also use it to inspect, diagnose, validate, preview, publish, or batch-render an existing HyperFrames project. Inputs may be a website URL, GitHub PR, Figma design or URL, text or brief, existing footage, or music. It resumes project state, captures intent when applicable, selects and installs the owning workflow, and routes domain capabilities. HyperFrames is the default output framework unless the user explicitly chooses another framework for the deliverable or asks only to record a browser session.
- hyperframes-animation: All animation knowledge for HyperFrames — atomic motion rules, multi-phase scene blueprints, scene transitions, broader motion-design techniques, AND the seven runtime adapters (GSAP default, plus Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, CSS keyframes, Web Animations API, TypeGPU). Use for any motion or animation task: pick 2-4 rules and compose, or load a blueprint, or look up runtime-specific API (e.g. GSAP eases / Lottie player / Three.js mixer). Also covers auditing an existing composition's choreography (animation map) and 24 named text-animation effects. HyperFrames-native: single paused timeline, seek-safe, deterministic.
- hyperframes-audio: Use when audio already placed in a HyperFrames composition needs to be mixed: fade-in/fade-out, crossfade, track gain or volume, volume automation, ducking, a music bed that fights a voiceover (voiceover carve), effects on a track (EQ, compressor, limiter, gate, saturation, delay, reverb, chorus, phaser, bitcrush), or automation envelopes drawn on a track's volume or any effect parameter. Don't use for sourcing or generating audio — finding BGM, SFX, or making a voiceover is `/media-use`. Don't use for clip timing or track layout, which is `/hyperframes-core`.
- hyperframes-cli: Use the HyperFrames CLI development loop: init, add, catalog, capture, lint, check, snapshot, compare, grade-compare, preview, play, present, beats, keyframes, single or batch render, publish, cloud, cloudrun, feedback, lambda, doctor, browser, info, upgrade, skills, compositions, docs, benchmark, telemetry, transcribe, auth, tts, and remove-background. Also use when diagnosing build or render failures. validate, inspect, and layout are deprecated aliases; use check. Covers local, HeyGen-hosted cloud, AWS Lambda, and Google Cloud Run rendering.
- hyperframes-core: The HyperFrames composition contract — build one renderable project. Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. Also covers Tailwind projects and the STORYBOARD.md / SCRIPT.md plan formats. Read before writing composition HTML.
- hyperframes-creative: Non-animation creative direction for HyperFrames videos. Use for design spec (frame.md / design.md) handling, palettes, typography, narration, beat planning, audio-reactive visuals, composition patterns, and brand / style decisions. For atomic motion patterns and scene blueprints, use `hyperframes-animation`.
- hyperframes-keyframes: Use when a HyperFrames composition needs a punch-in, punch-out, zoom, reframe, Ken Burns treatment, camera move, visual match/whip handoff, or other seek-safe 2D/3D keyframes; also for GSAP, CSS keyframes, Anime.js, WAAPI, FLIP, paths, masks, SVG morph/draw, text trails, 3D depth, or `hyperframes keyframes` diagnostics. Don't use for broad scene strategy, brand design, media sourcing, captions, or general video planning.
- hyperframes-registry: Install, discover, and wire registry blocks and components into HyperFrames compositions. Use when running hyperframes add or hyperframes catalog, installing one item or every block matching a tag, wiring an installed item into index.html, or working with hyperframes.json. Covers discovery, install locations, block sub-composition wiring, component snippet merging, and authoring a new block or component to contribute upstream (idea → scaffold → validate → PR).
- media-use: Agent Media OS, the single skill for every media need in a HyperFrames project. Resolve BGM, SFX, image, icon, brand logo, voice, color grade, or LUT into a frozen local file or paste-ready block + ledger record (one verb, `resolve`); generate via TTS / music / image models when the catalog misses; produce voiceover, transcription, captions, and background removal through one shared audio engine; operate on media (cut / reframe / transform); and reuse assets across projects. Also use for vague feedback that real footage looks dark, flat, boring, should feel retro/camcorder/print/ASCII, needs privacy, or needs a media reveal.
- motion-graphics: A short, design-led motion graphic where motion is the message — kinetic typography, stat count-up, chart/data-viz hit, logo sting / brand lockup, lower-third / callout / social overlay, animated map (highlight regions, connect places, zoom to a location), animated tweet / news-article / headline, webpage / UI animation (scroll, cursor, callouts), or fusing a real image's geometry into a chart. Usually under 10s (up to ~30s), no narration or live-action subject; renders to MP4 or transparent overlay. Longer / narrated / multi-scene → /general-video. Unclear → /hyperframes.

Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. The full billing model, plainly.", 5 "category": "Explainers", 6 "targetKeyword": "ai website builder credits", 7 "body": [ 8 "

Credit systems in AI tools are usually vague on purpose. A \"credit\" turns out to be an internal unit nobody can convert into money, the cost per action isn't stated, and you find out what things cost by running out. Here's Kodely's, defined precisely enough that you can check it.

", 9 10 "

A credit is a fixed amount of real model spend

", 11 "

One credit is $0.002 of the underlying model cost — so 500 credits is one dollar's worth. It isn't an abstract token, an action count, or a unit that means different things on different plans. It's a unit of the actual spend that a generation incurs.

", 12 "

New accounts get 750 credits free, with no card required.

", 13 14 "

You're charged from what a build actually used

", 15 "

Kodely doesn't charge a flat fee per build. When a generation finishes, the real token usage is measured — input, output, and cache reads and writes — priced at the model's published rate, and converted into credits at the rate above.

", 16 "

A small tweak to one section genuinely costs less than building a whole page from scratch, because it genuinely used fewer tokens. That's the point of metering rather than guessing.

", 17 18 "

A build that fails costs nothing

", 19 "

If the generated code doesn't compile — after one automatic repair attempt — the build is recorded with its true cost and charged zero credits. Not discounted. Zero.

", 20 "

This is structural, not a policy someone applies afterwards: credits are only ever deducted on a build's success path. The tokens spent on a failed build are real money that Kodely absorbs. More on what failure looks like from your side.

", 21 22 "

Some things never cost credits at all

", 23 "
  • Enhance. The button that expands a one-line idea into a full editable brief is free and isn't recorded as a build. A preview of what you're about to spend on shouldn't itself cost anything.
  • Rolling back. Restoring an earlier checkpoint from the History tab restores a snapshot you already paid for. It isn't a generation, so it isn't charged.
  • Publishing and republishing. Putting the site live, and putting an updated version live, cost nothing.
  • Downloading your source as a zip. Free, any number of times.
", 24 25 "

Why we don't quote a price per build

", 26 "

Here's the part most pages in this category would skip.

", 27 "

We don't publish a \"typical build costs N credits\" figure, and we're not going to until we can stand behind one. The measurements we have vary by roughly a factor of three depending on how much site is being built, and a handful of samples is not a distribution.

", 28 "

Quoting a precise-sounding average from that would be false confidence, and it would fail in the worst available direction: quote low, charge high, on a product whose entire pitch is that you won't be surprised by the bill. So the number stays unpublished until there's real data behind it — and when it appears it will move in whichever direction the evidence points, not the direction that markets better.

", 29 "

What you get instead is specific to you. The editor and dashboard show a running \"about this many builds left\" figure calculated from your own recent successful builds rather than a global constant. Someone building simple one-section pages and someone building dense ten-section pages deserve different answers to that question, and averaging their own history is the only honest way to give it. Until you've run a build, it falls back to a deliberately conservative estimate — over-promising how many builds you have left is how someone hits zero mid-generation.

", 30 31 "

You can set your own ceiling

", 32 "

The rules above stop any single build overcharging you. None of them stop you running thirty builds in an afternoon and being genuinely surprised by the total.

", 33 "

So you can set a spending cap in Settings: a maximum number of credits over a rolling 30-day window. Hit it and generation stops with a message saying it's your own cap and where to change it — never presented as a limit we imposed on you.

", 34 "

It's a rolling window rather than a calendar month on purpose. There's no reset day to game, and no cliff where the cap silently stops protecting you halfway through a month.

", 35 36 "

Warnings come before the wall, not at it

", 37 "

When your balance drops below roughly two builds' worth — measured against your own build history — the balance indicator turns amber and offers a top-up inline. The intent is that you never discover the problem in the middle of a generation.

", 38 "

Credits are bought in packs; current pack sizes and prices are on the pricing page. There's no subscription to forget about and no monthly minimum.

", 39 40 "

The four rules, in one place

", 41 "
  1. A credit is a fixed, published amount of real model spend — 500 credits to the dollar.
  2. You're charged from metered usage after a build succeeds, never from a flat guess.
  3. A build that fails is charged zero.
  4. You can cap your own spend over a rolling 30 days.
", 42 "

If any of those ever stops being true, it will be because we changed the product and said so — not because a definition quietly drifted.

", 43 "

Start with 750 free credits, or read what actually happens during a build.

" 44 ] 45 } 46

1 { 2 "slug": "how-to-build-a-barber-shop-website-with-ai", 3 "title": "How to Build a Barber Shop Website With AI", 4 "metaDescription": "A practical guide to getting a barber shop online in an afternoon — the prompt to write, how to handle bookings honestly, and what to expect.", 5 "category": "Guides", 6 "targetKeyword": "barber shop website builder", 7 "body": [ 8 "

A barber shop's website has one job: convince someone nearby that this is the place, then get them to book. Everything else is decoration. This guide covers building exactly that page with Kodely, and it is honest about the one thing you should not try to build into it.

", 9 10 "

The shape of the page

", 11 "

Kodely builds single-page sites, which suits this perfectly. A barber shop page that works usually goes:

", 12 "
  1. Shop name, the neighbourhood, and a booking button that is impossible to miss.
  2. A short line on what kind of cut you do — scissor work, skin fades, hot towel shaves, beard trims.
  3. Services and prices, as a clean list.
  4. The barbers, by name.
  5. Hours, address, and a big tappable phone number.
", 13 "

That's the whole thing. Most people are on a phone, deciding in under twenty seconds, so the price list and the booking button matter far more than the copywriting.

", 14 15 "

Bookings: the one thing to get right

", 16 "

Kodely generates the front end of a website. There is no server, no database, and no email sending behind it. So a booking form on your site would be a form that silently throws every appointment away.

", 17 "

So don't ask for one. Ask for a booking form and you may well get a handsome one that discards every appointment. What you do instead:

", 18 "
  • If you already use a booking platform, point a big \"Book now\" button straight at your booking page there.
  • If you take bookings by phone, make the number a tel: link so a tap dials it.
  • If you take them over Instagram or WhatsApp, link to that profile.
", 19 "

An outbound link is a navigation, not something the page loads from another server, so it works exactly as you'd expect. Put the destination in your prompt — \"the Book now button links to my booking page\" — and you'll get a real, working call-to-action.

", 20 21 "

Write the prompt

", 22 "

The more concrete you are about the shop, the less generic the result. Anything factual you leave out — prices, hours, your barbers' names — gets filled in with something plausible that you'll then have to correct, so bring it all.

", 23 "

A one-page site for Sharps & Co, a two-chair barber shop on Union Street. Traditional but not gimmicky — no handlebar-moustache clichés. Services: skin fade 22, scissor cut 20, beard trim 12, cut and beard 30, kids under 12 15. Two barbers, Danny and Ade. Open Tue-Sat 9-6, closed Sunday and Monday. Walk-ins welcome but booking preferred. Big \"Book now\" button at the top and bottom linking out to our booking page, and the phone number as a tap-to-call link. Dark charcoal background, warm off-white text, one amber accent colour, bold condensed headings.

", 24 "

If writing that feels like work, type one line and press Enhance. It expands your idea into a fuller brief that you read and edit before building. Enhance costs no credits.

", 25 26 "

What it will look like

", 27 "

There will be no photographs of your shop. Published Kodely sites run under a security policy that blocks requests to any other host, which rules out stock photography and remote images entirely. Typography, colour, spacing and inline SVG shapes do the visual work instead.

", 28 "

For a barber shop this is less of a loss than it sounds — a confident dark palette with strong type reads more like a real shop than a stock photo of someone else's chair. Every site is responsive down to a 380px-wide phone and ships with a dark mode treatment by default.

", 29 30 "

Iterate in plain English

", 31 "

The first build appears in a live preview. Then you refine it by asking, in the same box:

", 32 "
  • \"Put the price list above the barbers section.\"
  • \"Make the Book now button stick to the bottom of the screen on mobile.\"
  • \"Add 'Under-12s half price on Tuesdays' under the kids' cut.\"
  • \"The amber is too orange — take it towards gold.\"
", 33 "

Every successful build is saved as a checkpoint in the History tab, and rolling back to one is free. You are never one bad edit away from losing a version you liked.

", 34 35 "

Going live

", 36 "

One click publishes the compiled site to a kodely.site subdomain. Kodely also generates robots.txt and sitemap.xml, and guarantees the page has a real title and description so it looks right in a search result and in a link preview.

", 37 "

You can also download the whole source project as a zip at any point — it's a standard Vite project, so a developer can take it anywhere later without asking us for anything.

", 38 39 "

Cost

", 40 "

You start with 750 free credits and no card on file. Credits are charged from measured model usage after a build succeeds; a build that fails to compile costs you nothing. You can also set your own rolling 30-day spending cap so the total can never surprise you.

", 41 "

Start with your shop name, your price list and your hours — that's enough for a first version. See also: how to write a prompt that gets a good first build.

" 42 ] 43 } 44

AI Website Builder for Dentists
Build a professional dental practice website in minutes with Kodely's AI website builder. Real code, live preview, and a free live URL, no coding required.
What a dental practice site actually needs to do

Most people who land on your website aren't browsing — they're deciding whether to book. They want to know, in about ten seconds, whether you take their insurance, where you're located, whether you have appointments this week, and whether other patients trust you. If your site loads slowly, looks dated, or buries that information behind three clicks, they'll open a new tab and call the next dentist on the list instead.

That's the bar: fast, professional, mobile-friendly, and organized around what a nervous or busy patient actually wants to find. You don't need a flashy site. You need the right sections, done well, live today instead of "sometime next quarter" once a web designer gets to it.


The sections your practice site can't skip


Services

List what you actually do — cleanings, whitening, crowns, Invisalign, emergency care, pediatric dentistry, whatever applies. Vague copy like "comprehensive dental care" doesn't help patients or search engines. Name the procedures. Patients searching "emergency tooth extraction near me" need to see that phrase, or something close to it, on your site.


About / meet the dentist

A short bio, a real photo, credentials, and how long you've been practicing. Dental visits are personal and a little nerve-wracking for a lot of people — a face and a few sentences of context do more to build trust than another stock photo of a smiling model.


Location and hours

Full address, a map, parking notes if relevant, and hours that are correct and easy to scan. This sounds obvious, but it's the single most common thing broken or out of date on small-practice websites.


Appointment request

A simple form where a patient enters their name, contact info, preferred day/time, and reason for the visit. Kodely can build you a genuinely good-looking, professional appointment-request page and contact form. To be clear about what that means today: it collects the request and sends it to you — it does not yet sync automatically to a calendar or scheduling system. Most small practices are fine with this as a starting point: the request comes in, your front desk confirms by phone or email, same as an inquiry from any other channel.


Patient reviews

A dedicated section with a handful of real testimonials, plus a clear link out to your Google Business Profile where the full review history lives. Reviews are one of the biggest trust signals for a first-time patient, and they help local search too.


A prompt you can copy and use right now

Kodely builds from plain-English descriptions typed into a chat box — the more specific you are, the better the first draft. Here's an example for a fictional practice, Willow Creek Dental, that you can adapt with your own details:

Prompt: "Build a website for Willow Creek Dental, a family dentistry practice in Bend, Oregon. We offer general checkups and cleanings, teeth whitening, Invisalign, and emergency dental care. Use a clean, calming design in soft blues and white, with a warm, welcoming feel — not clinical or cold. Include a homepage with a hero section and a clear call-to-action to request an appointment, a Services section listing our four services with short descriptions, an About section introducing Dr. Elena Marsh with a short bio, a Location and Hours section with our address (412 Larch Street, Bend, OR) and Monday-Friday 8am-5pm hours, an appointment request form asking for name, phone, email, preferred date, and reason for visit, and a Patient Reviews section with three sample testimonials. Make it fully mobile-friendly."

That single prompt is usually enough for a solid first version. From there you keep chatting: "make the hero image bigger," "add a Insurance We Accept section," "change the accent color to teal" — each change edits the real components Kodely already generated, and you can preview the result immediately.


What you actually get when it's done


Real code, not a template. Kodely generates an actual Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS app with its own component files — a genuine foundation you can keep building on, not a locked-down theme with swapped colors.

Live preview as you build. You see the actual compiled site update while you describe changes, not a mockup.

A free live URL. One click publishes your site to willowcreekdental.kodely.site (or your practice's name) — included at no extra cost. There's no custom-domain support yet, so for now your site lives at that address.

Checkpoints. Every successful generation is a save point. If a change doesn't look right, roll back for free and try a different instruction.

Code view. You can see and copy the generated source directly in the app. Full project export as a downloadable zip isn't available yet.

Ongoing edits by chat. Adding a new service, updating your hours, swapping a testimonial — all done by describing the change, no code editor required.



Tips for local SEO once your site is live


Keep your name, address, and phone number identical everywhere they appear — your website, Google Business Profile, and any directory listings. Inconsistent details hurt local rankings.

Claim and fully fill out your Google Business Profile and link to it from your site. For most dental searches, this listing gets seen before the website does.

Use the actual service names patients search for — "dental implants," "root canal," "same-day crowns" — in your Services section headings, not just marketing language.

Mention your city and neighborhood in the copy, not just the address block. "Family dentist in Bend, Oregon" reads naturally and helps local search understand what you do and where.

Make sure it's fast and mobile-friendly. A large share of "dentist near me" searches happen on a phone, often from someone already in pain — a slow site loses that visitor immediately.

Ask happy patients for reviews and keep the testimonials on your site current. Fresh, specific reviews (not generic ones) perform better with both patients and search engines.



FAQ


Can Kodely build online booking for my dental practice?

Kodely can build a professional, well-designed appointment-request page and contact form. It collects the patient's request — it doesn't yet connect to a real calendar or scheduling backend automatically, so your team confirms the appointment manually, the same way you'd handle a phone or email inquiry.


Can I use my own domain, like willowcreekdental.com?

Not yet. Right now every published site lives at a free yourname.kodely.site address. Custom domain support isn't available yet.


Do I need to know how to code?

No. You describe what you want in plain English, and Kodely writes and updates the actual code for you. If you're curious, you can open the code view to see and copy the generated source, but it's never required.


How much does it cost to build a dentist website with Kodely?

New accounts get 750 free credits with no card required, and a typical first build for a site like this runs roughly 100-150 credits — enough for several iterations while you get the sections right. If you need more, top-ups start at $9 for 500 credits, with a $40 pack for 2,500 credits and a $90 pack for 6,000 credits; credits never expire. Builds that fail to compile aren't charged. See pricing for full details.


Can I export the code and host it myself?

Not yet — there's no zip download or export option today. You can view and copy source from the in-app code view, and publish directly to your free kodely.site address.


How do I get started?

Create a free account at sign up — no card required — and describe your practice the way it's shown in the example prompt above. If you already have an account, log in and start a new project. For more examples and tips, browse the blog, or head to the homepage to see what else Kodely can build.

What chiropractors actually need from a website

Chiropractic patients are usually dealing with pain, and pain makes people impatient. Someone searching "chiropractor near me" at 11pm with a stiff back wants three things fast: proof you're legitimate, proof you're close by and open, and an obvious way to reach you. Everything else — your philosophy of care, your equipment, your Instagram feed — is secondary to those three jobs.

Services

Give each service its own short block so both patients and Google can match a search to a specific page.


About

# Corrections to live blog posts

The 56 posts on kodely.me have no source in this repo. Their only source of
truth is the `BlogPost` table on the production box. `seo-batch1.json` holds
14 of them and is a *snapshot*, not the source — it is left untouched, because
editing it would create a second thing that looks authoritative and isn't.

So a correction here is a surgical, literal find-and-replace against a live
row, run by `scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs`. Each file in this directory is one
group of related corrections.

## The three groups

| file | gate | what it fixes |
|---|---|---|
| `credit-figure.json` | none | Removes the published "a typical first build runs 100–150 credits" figure. **No number replaces it.** |
| `capability-claims.json` | none | Posts promising a working booking/contact form, a multi-page site, or photos you add later. |
| `export-claim.json` | `export-shipped` | Inverts "there is no zip or full-project download" — **only valid once the export route deploys.** |

## Read this before touching `export-claim`

`app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts`, `lib/zip.ts` and the **Download .zip**
button in `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` are all **untracked in git**. The
feature is built and not deployed. That means every "there is no zip export"
sentence on kodely.me is **true right now**.

It stops being true the moment that code ships. There is no ordering that is
safe on either side of the deploy:

- run it early and ~30 live pages advertise a button that does not exist;
- run it late and ~30 live pages tell a developer evaluating the product that
  the thing they are looking at cannot be exported. Two of them
  (`kodely-vs-rocket-new`, `kodely-vs-lovable`) print it in a comparison table
  as a column where a competitor wins.

**Ship the corrections in the same deploy window as the export route.** The
`--gate export-shipped` flag exists so that running the corrector on a normal
day cannot do this by accident: the group is skipped, loudly, unless the
operator asserts the gate on the command line.

## Procedure

Run everything from a checkout on the production box, with `DATABASE_URL`
pointing at the production database.

### 1. Before the deploy — the two ungated groups

```
node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group credit-figure --group capability-claims
```

Read the whole dry run. Three things to look for:

- **`change`** lines — the before/after of every edit. Read the `+` text.
- **`STALE`** — neither the old text nor the new text is in the row. The live
  copy has drifted from what these files were written against. Fix the edit
  against the real row; do not force anything.
- **`RESIDUE`** — a row still matching the group's `detect` patterns after the
  planned edits. This is the part that catches the 42 live posts this repo has
  no copy of. Every residue line is a place still making the claim.

For residue, get the exact current text and write a replacement:

```
node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group credit-figure --emit-stubs
```

That writes `content/seo/corrections/pending.generated.json` with the exact
matched text as `find` and an empty `replace`. Fill each `replace` in, move the
entries into the right group file, delete the generated file, re-run the dry
run. Repeat until the sweep is clean.

Then apply:

```
node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group credit-figure --group capability-claims --apply
```

The script exits non-zero while any stale edit or residue remains, so a clean
exit code is the signal that the whole class is gone — not just the rows
somebody remembered.

### 2. In the export deploy window

Immediately after the deploy that ships the export route, in the same window:

```
node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group export-claim
node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group export-claim --apply
```

Then confirm, with the same command, that the sweep is clean. Anything left is
a page still denying a feature you just shipped.

`app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` is `force-static` with `revalidate = 3600`, so a
corrected page can take up to an hour to change for visitors. That is worth
knowing before someone concludes the script did nothing.

## Properties the corrector guarantees

- **Literal matches only.** No regex ever rewrites live prose. An edit that no
  longer matches changes nothing and is reported as `STALE`.
- **Idempotent.** An edit already applied is `already corrected` and skipped.
  Only `bodyHtml` is written, so `@updatedAt` does not churn on a re-run.
- **Non-destructive.** Update-by-slug only. No create path, no delete path.
- **It checks its own work.** The `detect` sweep runs over *every* row in the
  table, including posts no correction file names.

Here is why Kodely gives you a mailto, a tel link and a link-out instead.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "ai website builder contact form", "body": [ "

Ask almost any AI website builder for a contact form and you will get one. It will have a name field, an email field, a message box, a submit button, and a little \"Thanks, we'll be in touch!\" state that appears when you click it. It will look completely convincing.

", "

On a site with no backend, none of that is real. The message goes nowhere. Nobody is told. The person who typed it watches a confirmation appear and reasonably concludes you have their enquiry.

", "

That is the failure this page is about, and it is worth understanding properly, because it is the single most expensive mistake you can make with a generated site.

", "

What a form actually needs

", "

A working form is three things, not one. There is the visible part — the inputs and the button. Then there is somewhere to send the submission: a server endpoint that accepts it. Then there is something that acts on it: a database row, an email, a notification.

", "

An AI builder that generates front-end code produces the first of those three. A Kodely project is a Vite, React, TypeScript and Tailwind application — real component files, compiled server-side into static output. There is no server process in it, because there is nothing in it that runs on a server. The whole thing is HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs in your visitor's browser.

", "

So the second and third parts do not exist and cannot be added by rephrasing the prompt. This is not a limit of how clearly you asked.

", "

Even the network call is blocked

", "

There is a second layer to this that people are usually surprised by. Suppose you decided to wire the form up yourself to some third-party form service. A published Kodely site is served under a strict content security policy, and one of its directives is connect-src 'none'.

", "

That directive means the page is not permitted to make network requests to anywhere at all — not to another host, not to a form endpoint, not to an analytics collector. The browser refuses it before the request leaves the machine.

", "

The policy exists so that a published site can only ever be itself. Nothing it renders can phone home, load a tracker, or pull a script from somewhere that got compromised last Tuesday. That is a genuinely good property. It also means a form has no escape hatch.

", "

What to build instead

", "

Everything a small site actually needs from a contact form can be done with a link, and a link is a navigation rather than a request, so it works perfectly:

", "
  • A mailto: link. Opens the visitor's mail app with your address already filled in. You can prefill a subject line too, so enquiries arrive pre-sorted.
  • A tel: link. On a phone, a tap dials you. For a local business this converts better than any form ever has.
  • A link out to a tool that has a backend. Your booking system, your scheduling page, your WhatsApp or Instagram profile, your ticketing page. Those platforms have servers. Send people to them.
", "

Label them for what they do. \"Email us\", \"Call now\", \"Book on [your booking platform]\" — never a bare \"Submit\", which implies something is being submitted.

", "

Inside the built-in catalogue of icons, gradients, flags and textures a Kodely site draws from.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "ai website builder icons", "body": [ "

A published Kodely site cannot load anything from another host. No icon font, no CDN, no image URL, no npm package added at build time. And yet the pages have icons, textures, gradients and dividers in them.

", "

Where do those come from? It is a more interesting answer than \"the model draws them\", and it explains a visible change in how generated sites look.

", "

The problem with a model drawing its own icons

", "

Left to itself, a language model asked for a phone icon writes SVG path data from scratch. Sometimes that works. Often it produces something that is recognisably phone-shaped and subtly wrong: inconsistent stroke weights across a set, an optical size that does not match its neighbours, a curve that kinks.

", "

It is also expensive. Path data is dense, arbitrary numbers — some of the most token-hungry text a model can generate, and every one of those tokens is metered as part of what your build costs.

", "

So hand-drawn geometry was the worst of both: less consistent than a real icon set, and dearer than one.

", "

A catalogue the builder searches

", "

Instead, Kodely ships a catalogue of inlinable assets and gives the builder a tool to search it in plain words. Ask for \"plumber wrench icon\", \"warm sunset gradient\" or \"wave divider\" and it gets back paste-ready source it drops straight into a component.

", "

What is in it:

", "
  • 147 icons, categorised — contact, social, commerce, food, trades and interface — drawn as a consistent set with a shared stroke weight, and coloured by currentColor so they inherit the text colour around them.
  • 250 countries, 55 of them with hand-drawn inline SVG flags and the rest as flag characters.
  • 30 gradients and 30 mesh backgrounds, which do the job a hero photograph would do elsewhere.
  • 12 section dividers — waves, angles, torn edges — for the transitions between bands of colour.
  • 12 CSS patterns and 3 grain textures, for surfaces that need not to be flat.
  • Initials avatars, generated from a name, for the places a headshot would normally sit.
", "

Every one of those is markup, CSS or a data: URI. Nothing fetches anything, which is what makes them safe under a policy that blocks every other host.

", "

What this changes about the output

", "

Three things, in rough order of how much you will notice them:

", "
  1. Consistency. Six icons from one set look like a set. Six improvised ones look like six decisions.
  2. Cost. Pasting a catalogue entry is dramatically fewer tokens than generating path data, and builds are charged from measured token usage rather than a flat fee — so this shows up in what you pay.
  3. Ambition. Mesh backgrounds, grain and dividers are the difference between a page of white boxes and a page with a designed surface. They are also exactly the things a model will not improvise well.
", "

You can ask for specific things

Since the builder searches the catalogue in plain words, your prompt can steer it. Useful things to say:

  • \"Put a subtle grain texture over the dark sections.\"
  • \"Icons for each service — spanner, boiler, radiator.\"
  • \"A warm mesh gradient behind the hero instead of a flat colour.\"
", "

And things worth avoiding: asking for a specific commercial icon set by name, or for a brand logo. Neither is in the catalogue and neither can be fetched.

", "

What it still does not solve

", "

Being clear about the boundary: this is artwork, not photography. There is no photograph of your shop, your food, your team or your work, because no image can be loaded from another host and there is no upload path. A catalogue of icons and gradients does not change that.

What it does change is how good the alternative looks. A page built from real typography, a considered palette, a mesh background and a coherent icon set is a designed page. That is a different thing from a page that is visibly missing its photographs.

{ "slug": "what-a-published-ai-site-is-allowed-to-load", "title": "What a Published AI Site Is Allowed to Load", "metaDescription": "The exact security policy every published Kodely site runs under, what each directive rules out, and why that is mostly good news.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "ai website builder security policy", "body": [ "

Most of the surprising limits of an AI-built site trace back to a single line of configuration. Rather than explain them one at a time, here is the line itself, and what each part of it means for a page you publish.

", "

Every published Kodely site is served with this content security policy:

", "

default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'

", "

Six directives. Between them they decide almost everything about what your site can be.

", "

Reading it directive by directive

", "
  • default-src 'self' — the fallback for everything not named below. Resources may only come from the site's own origin. No CDN, no third-party host, ever.
  • style-src and script-src, both 'self' 'unsafe-inline' — the site's own CSS and JavaScript run, including inline. A compiled React app needs this.
  • img-src 'self' data: — images may come from the site itself or be embedded as data: URIs. This is why inline SVG works and a remote image URL does not.
  • connect-src 'none' — the strongest one. The page may make no network requests at all. No fetch, no XHR, no WebSocket, to anywhere, including its own origin.
  • frame-ancestors 'self' — nobody else can embed your site in a frame on their page.
", "

What each one rules out in practice

", "

No form can submit anything. That is connect-src 'none' doing its job, on top of the more basic fact that there is no server behind the site to receive a submission. Even wiring a form by hand to a third-party endpoint would fail in the browser. The consequences, and what to build instead.

", "

No analytics, no chat widget, no tracking pixel. All of those are a script from another host, a network request, or both.

", "

No photographs from anywhere else. img-src permits the site's own files and data: URIs only, and there is no upload path to make a photo one of the site's own files. Why that is the case.

", "

No embedded video or streaming player. Same reason.

", "

No map embed. A map is a script and a stream of image tiles from another host. Put the address on the page as text instead — which is better for search anyway — and link out to a maps app.

", "

The font one, which surprises everybody

", "

There is no font-src directive in that policy. That does not mean fonts are unrestricted; it means fonts fall back to default-src 'self'.

", "

So a font from a hosting service is blocked, which people expect. But a font embedded as a base64 data: URI is also blocked, which almost nobody expects — because img-src explicitly allows data: and default-src does not.

", "

The practical result: type comes from the system font stack. On a Mac or iPhone that is the Apple system face; on Windows it is Segoe UI; elsewhere it falls back sensibly. Those are good typefaces, and they load instantly because they are already on the device. But if your brand depends on a specific licensed font, this is the constraint to weigh before you start.

", "

Why have the policy at all

", "

Because the alternative is worse in ways that are easy to miss.

", "

A site generated from a prompt is code written by a model. Most of the time that code is fine. The policy is what makes \"most of the time\" acceptable: even if something got through that tried to load a remote script, the browser refuses it. A published site cannot exfiltrate what a visitor types, cannot pull in a script from a host that gets compromised next year, and cannot quietly start tracking people.

", "

It also makes the sites genuinely fast, for the unglamorous reason that a page which cannot make requests has nothing to wait for. No render-blocking font, no analytics on the critical path, no third-party script deciding your load time.

", "

Deciding whether this suits you

", "

The honest test is one question: does your site's job depend on something outside itself?

", "

If it needs photography, live data, payments, analytics or an embedded booking widget in the page, the answer is yes, and you should know that before you build rather than after. If its job is to be a fast, credible page that says who you are and sends people to the right place — which is most small sites — the policy costs you very little and buys you a lot.

", "

Build one and see — 750 free credits, no card required. See also: the full list of what Kodely cannot build yet, and what it uses for artwork instead.

" ] }

Which one you need, and what changes when you own the page instead of renting it.", "category": "Comparisons", "targetKeyword": "link in bio vs website", "body": [ "

", "

", "

What a link list is genuinely good at

", "

", "

", "

Where a list stops being enough

", "

Four situations, and you will recognise yours immediately:

", "
  1. Someone needs to be persuaded, not routed. A list cannot say what you do, who it is for, or why you are good at it. If people arrive not yet convinced, a list asks them to click before they have a reason to.
  2. You want to be found. A hosted profile page is thin content on somebody else's domain. It is not going to rank for \"plumber in [your town]\" — a page with your services, your area names and your credentials in real text has a chance.
  3. You need to say more than a label. Prices, hours, what is included, what you do not do. That is content, and a list has nowhere to put it.
  4. It is your address on printed things. A van, a card, a menu. That URL wants to be yours and to look like a business.
", "

The ownership difference

", "

The structural point, and the one people feel later rather than sooner.

", "

A hosted profile is a tenancy. The design, the URL shape, the features and the terms belong to the platform, and the page is intelligible only inside it.

", "

A Kodely site is a real application: Vite, React, TypeScript and Tailwind, compiled to static files. There is a code view where you can read exactly what was generated — actual component files, not an abstraction of them. That is a different kind of thing to have, even if you never open it. What \"real code\" does and does not mean.

", "

What a one-page site costs you in exchange

Being even-handed about our own side:

  • Some things are not buildable. No forms, no payments, no photographs, no analytics. A published site runs under a policy that blocks every other host. Link-outs cover most of it; not all.
  • The address is a subdomain for now. Custom domains are not supported yet, which matters if you are printing it on something.
", "

The honest middle

", "

You can build a one-page site that is mostly a link list and slightly more: a real headline that says what you do, one paragraph, then the buttons. That page routes as well as a list, ranks better than one, and looks like a business rather than a profile.

", "

It is also the fastest thing to build, because the content is short and the structure is obvious. If you are unsure which side you are on, that is the version to make.

", "

Choosing

", "
  • Link list if your audience already knows who you are and only needs forwarding.
  • One-page site if strangers arrive, if you want search traffic, or if the URL goes on anything physical.
  • Both is fine. They are not in competition — the list can be one of the links on your page, or the other way round.
", "

Build the one-page version with 750 free credits and see which one you keep. See also: when one page stops being enough.

" ] }

What a social profile does better

  2. The stuff nobody posts. Prices, hours, service area, insurance, what you do not do. On a profile it is buried in a post from March. On a page it is a section.

The part these comparisons usually skip.

What the site actually needs to contain

Deciding

content.text:
Both hard gates are clean. Here's the report.

## What I built (all inside `content/seo/` and `scripts/seo/`)

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs` | Surgical, literal, idempotent find-and-replace against live `BlogPost` rows, with a self-verifying sweep |
| `scripts/seo/check-claims.mjs` | Claim linter — encodes the product's real limits as patterns, each citing the source file that decides it |
| `content/seo/corrections/credit-figure.json` | 21 edits / 14 slugs, ungated |
| `content/seo/corrections/capability-claims.json` | 10 edits / 3 slugs, ungated |
| `content/seo/corrections/export-claim.json` | 37 edits / 26 slugs, **gated behind `--gate export-shipped`** |
| `content/seo/corrections/README.md` | The prod runbook |
| 17 new articles in `content/seo/` | Batch 3 |

`seo-batch1.json` was read, never edited — it's a snapshot of 14 of the 56 live posts, not their source, and editing it would create a second thing that looks authoritative and isn't. `app/blog/**`, `lib/`, `prisma/`, `proxy.ts`, `deploy.sh`, `.env`, `package.json` untouched.

## PART 1 — corrections

### The credit figure (21 occurrences, 14 posts)

The 56 live posts have no repo source, so I surveyed all of them against the live site. The figure appears in **five different phrasings** — `100–150` (en dash), `100-150` (hyphen), `100 to 150` (spelled out), `in the 100–150 credit range`, `typically costs 100–150`. A single regex would have missed a third of them; a regex *rewrite* would have mangled prose. So every edit is an exact literal string, and every one I could verify against a local copy was verified before shipping.

Representative before/after (all 21 are in the file with a `note` naming the grounding):

> **`kodely-vs-rocket-new`**
> − Credits don't expire. *A typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits, and a follow-up change is usually in the same range,* so the free tier is enough to actually build and iterate on something before you have to decide whether to pay.
> \+ Credits don't expire. *What a build costs is metered from its real model usage rather than charged as a flat fee, and a build that fails to compile is never charged at all* — so you can start building before deciding whether to pay.

> **`ai-website-builder-with-transparent-pricing`** (worst placement of the figure on the site)
> − A typical first build, the initial site generated from your description, runs roughly 100 to 150 credits.
> \+ What a build costs comes from its own measured token usage — input, output and cache — priced at the model's published rate, not from a flat per-build fee.

**I also removed every sufficiency claim derived from the number** — "enough for a first build plus several rounds of edits", "covers several real builds", "enough to build and iterate several times over". Those inherit the same bad arithmetic: at the observed 472-credit high, 750 credits is roughly one build and one edit, not several. Leaving them in would have preserved the understatement with the number deleted.

No replacement number anywhere. `estimateCredits`'s own comment is the authority: two samples is not a distribution.

### The export claim (37 occurrences, 26 posts) — gated

`app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts`, `lib/zip.ts` and the **Download .zip** button in `Editor.tsx` are **untracked in git**. Built, not deployed. Every "there is no zip export" sentence on kodely.me is true today.

The group will not run without `--gate export-shipped` on the command line, and the script prints why it skipped. Two of the corrections are comparison-table cells (`kodely-vs-rocket-new`, `kodely-vs-lovable`) where the current text hands the row to a competitor. One (`kodely-vs-webflow`) literally says *"the code lives inside Kodely until that export ships"* — a sentence that must not survive the deploy that makes it false.

Replacements never overclaim: the route streams the **draft source tree**, not build output, and there is still no GitHub sync, so every replacement says so.

### Procedure for prod

From a checkout on the production box with `DATABASE_URL` pointed at prod:

1. **Before the deploy:** `node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group credit-figure --group capability-claims` → read the dry run → `--apply`.
2. Three things to read in the output: `change` (before/after), `STALE` (live copy drifted — fix the edit, never force), `RESIDUE` (a row still matching the group's detect patterns *after* the planned edits — this is what covers the 42 live posts with no repo copy).
3. For residue: `--emit-stubs` writes `pending.generated.json` with the exact matched text as `find` and an empty `replace`. Fill them in, move them into the group file, re-run until the sweep is clean. The script exits non-zero while any stale edit or residue remains, so a clean exit code means the whole class is gone — not just the rows someone remembered.
4. **In the export deploy window, not after:** `node scripts/seo/correct-live.mjs --group export-claim --gate export-shipped --apply`.
5. `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` is `force-static` with `revalidate = 3600` — a corrected page takes up to an hour to change for visitors.

Guarantees: literal matches only (a stale edit changes nothing and reports), idempotent (only `bodyHtml` written, so `@updatedAt` doesn't churn), no create path and no delete path. I exercised dry-run → apply → re-run on a throwaway row in the **local** DB, then deleted the row and the test group; local table is back to its original 17.

## Verdict on the four suspect posts

All four are dishonest at the level of the keyword intent that brought the reader. Ranked by severity:

**1. `website-builder-for-dentists` — worst on the site.** It says the appointment form *"collects the request and sends it to you"*. There is no server and no mail path behind a generated site. That sentence tells a dental practice that patient appointment requests are arriving. They are not — they are discarded silently, and the patient sees a confirmation. It also instructs the reader to prompt for "a real photo" and "a map" (both impossible) and to ask for "three sample testimonials" for a real practice. Corrections written for the form claim, both instances.

**2. `website-builder-for-chiropractors`.** Same form failure, phrased as *"a genuinely good-looking, working request form"* plus *"have staff follow up on submissions"* — submissions that don't exist. Additionally its flagship example prompt asks for **four separate pages** ("Add a Services page… an About page… a Location & Hours page"), which contradicts the already-deployed `lib/agent.ts` rule *"this is a single-page app"*, and asks for 3–4 testimonials for a named practice. All three corrected.

**3. `website-builder-for-photographers`.** The most structurally dishonest, and it needs more than a sentence swap. It tells photographers the gallery *"ships with placeholder images"* and that *"after your site is live, you'll need to add your own photos yourself."* There is no path by which that ever happens — no upload, and `img-src 'self' data:` with `connect-src 'none'` blocks remote images permanently. The article's central promise is a step the product cannot perform, before or after any deploy. **My recommendation is rewrite or unpublish, not patch**: photography is the one vertical where the CSP removes the entire product. I did not write correction edits for it because there is no honest small change — the piece is 60% about a gallery that cannot exist. (I have no verbatim DB text for it either; it isn't in `seo-batch1.json`.)

**4. `build-a-booking-appointment-website-with-ai`.** Genuinely the most honest of the four about persistence — it says plainly that submissions aren't saved. It's still wrong in three ways: it recommends prompting for the form anyway ("It reads and behaves like a real booking flow"), it promises backend form delivery as *"coming in a future release"*, and it tells you to ask for testimonials and a hero background image. Corrected — the "what you get" list now leads with a link-out CTA, and the roadmap promise is removed rather than re-dated.

**Important wording note:** the working tree's `lib/agent.ts` adds "never invent facts about a real business" and "never build something that only pretends to work" — **HEAD has neither**, so they aren't deployed. Every correction replacement is deliberately phrased to be true before *and* after that ships: it states what a form on the site **does** (nothing), never what the builder currently agrees to draw.

Beyond the four, the survey turned up the same class elsewhere, which I did not have verbatim text to fix: `website-builder-for-restaurants` and `website-builder-for-accountants` both claim *"a multi-page app with working navigation"*; `website-builder-for-interior-designers` and `-restaurants` both say you swap placeholder visuals for your own photography afterwards; `ai-website-generator-from-a-description` claims *"a contact form with working input state"* with no backend caveat at all. The `capability-claims` detect patterns catch all of these on a prod run.

## PART 2 — 17 new articles

Every capability claim is grounded in code. All 34 files pass `validate.mjs` (0 failing, 0 warnings) and `check-claims.mjs` (0 errors).

**Guides — buildable verticals, one page, link-out CTAs:** coffee shop, food truck, gym/studio, cleaning business, wedding, event, nonprofit, band/musician, coming-soon page. Plus two how-tos: `how-to-add-a-booking-button-to-an-ai-built-site` and `starting-from-a-template-or-a-blank-prompt`.

**Explainers:** `why-ai-built-sites-have-no-contact-form`, `why-an-ai-builder-should-leave-blanks`, `where-the-icons-in-an-ai-built-site-come-from`, `what-a-published-ai-site-is-allowed-to-load`.

**Comparisons (only factual about Kodely's own side, no competitor claims at all):** `one-page-website-vs-a-link-in-bio-page`, `a-website-vs-a-facebook-page-for-a-local-business`.

Grounding by claim:
- CSP directives quoted verbatim → `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` `SANDBOX_CSP`
- no font, not even base64 → the `font-src` paragraph in `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM
- single page → SYSTEM "Multi-page: this is a single-page app"
- no forms / mailto / tel / link-out → no backend in `lib/foundation.ts` + `connect-src 'none'`
- bracketed placeholders → SYSTEM "Never invent facts about a real business"
- asset counts (**147 icons, 250 countries of which 55 have hand-drawn SVG flags, 30 gradients, 30 mesh backgrounds, 12 dividers, 12 CSS patterns, 3 grain textures**) → counted from `lib/assets/icons.ts`, `flags.ts`, `patterns.ts`. I did not publish a grand total; the SYSTEM prompt says "~460", my count of catalogue entries is 485, and I wasn't going to publish a number I couldn't reconcile.
- templates are prompts not layouts, and are written never to ask for a form/cart/second page/remote image/web font → the header comment and `description` fields in `lib/templates.ts` (23 templates)
- 750 free credits → `SIGNUP_GRANT`; failed builds charged zero → `creditsCharged: 0` on the FAILED branch of `app/api/generate/route.ts`; metered not flat → `costMicros`
- publish behaviour, `robots.txt`/`sitemap.xml`, title backstop → `lib/site-seo.ts`

**No per-build credit figure appears anywhere in the 17. No article mentions zip export at all** — mentioning it is false today and omitting it stays true after the deploy, so it was the only stable choice.

## What I could not write truthfully, and what needs your decision

1. **13 of the 17 pre-existing `content/seo` articles claim the zip download exists.** They are not live yet, so this isn't a public error — but seeding them before the export route deploys publishes 13 false claims. `node scripts/seo/check-claims.mjs` (no flags) lists them and exits 1. **Do not run `seed.mjs` for real until export ships**, or edit those sentences first.
2. **Batch 2 and batch 3 both assume the working tree, not HEAD.** `lib/enhance.ts`, `lib/assets/`, `lib/templates.ts`, `app/templates/`, `app/settings/` and the new `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM rules are all untracked or unmerged. All 17 existing articles reference Enhance; 12 of my 17 reference bracketed placeholders. Three of mine depend on undeployed code outright: `where-the-icons-in-an-ai-built-site-come-from` (needs `lib/assets`), `starting-from-a-template-or-a-blank-prompt` (needs `lib/templates` + `/templates`), `why-an-ai-builder-should-leave-blanks` (needs the new SYSTEM). **The whole of `content/seo` ships with that deploy or not at all.**
3. **Topics I refused:** anything needing a backend, form delivery, e-commerce, image upload, multi-page routing, custom domains, relaxed CSP or `font-src`. Specifically I did not write the obvious high-volume ones — photographer sites, online stores, contact-form guides, "add analytics to your AI site", "connect your domain".
4. **`website-builder-for-photographers` needs a rewrite decision from you**, not a patch. See the verdict above.
